items.title: The oceans absorb more CO2 than all forests combined
items.claim: Which is the larger annual carbon sink?

options.text: Oceans absorb around 25% of anthropogenic CO2 (around 2.5 GtC/year); land sinks (mainly forests) take up around 31%, but oceans hold by far the larger total reservoir
Neither — CO2 stays in the atmosphere

items.reveal:
Global Carbon Project annual budget: of around 10 GtC/year emitted by humans, around 25% goes to oceans, around 31% to land, and around 44% remains in the atmosphere (where it has driven the CO2 rise from 280 ppm pre-industrial to over 420 ppm).

Oceans absorb CO2 by both physical (cold water absorbing more) and biological (phytoplankton fixing carbon) pathways. The result is ocean acidification — pH has fallen by around 0.1 since pre-industrial, a 30% increase in H+ concentration.

Deforestation is itself a major source of CO2, partly offsetting the land sink.
items.why: Climate accounting is about budgets. Both sinks are essential — and both are at risk: ocean uptake is slowing as warming reduces solubility; land uptake is stressed by drought and fire.

items.title: The Amazon transpires its own rainfall
items.claim: How important is Amazon vegetation to its own rainfall?

options.text: Rainfall comes entirely from the Atlantic; vegetation is irrelevant
Trees transpire huge quantities of water vapour, generating 'flying rivers' that recycle moisture 5-6 times across the basin and supply rainfall to southeast South America
Rainfall is driven by Andean snowmelt
There is no rainfall in the Amazon

items.reveal:
A mature Amazon tree can transpire 200-1,000 litres a day. Antonio Nobre's 'flying rivers' concept (popularised through INPE Brazilian space agency research) describes the moisture flux from the basin to the south, equivalent to or greater than the Amazon River's discharge.

Deforestation reduces transpiration; some regions of the southern and eastern Amazon are already net carbon sources (Gatti et al., Nature 2021). A tipping point at perhaps 20-25% deforestation could shift large parts of the forest to savannah, with knock-on effects on Brazilian agriculture.
items.why: Forests are climate machines, not passive vegetation cover. The Amazon's ecological role is hydrological as much as biological — and its loss would change rainfall patterns far outside the basin.

items.title: Bankfull discharge has a return period of around 1-2 years

options.text: The discharge that fills the channel to the top of its banks — for most rivers, with a return period of around 1-2 years; this is the flow most responsible for channel shape (the 'dominant discharge')

items.reveal:
Bankfull is the discharge at which water just begins to spill onto the floodplain. Wolman and Miller (1960) showed that this 'effective' discharge does most of the geomorphic work, because it combines moderate magnitude with sufficient frequency.

Flood frequency analysis fits a probability distribution (often Gumbel or GEV) to the annual maximum series. A 100-year flood has a 1% chance of occurring in any year — not a guaranteed schedule.

Flood Estimation Handbook methods (UK) and Bulletin 17C (US) standardise flood frequency analysis. Urbanisation 'flashifies' hydrographs — peak discharge rises and lag time falls.
items.why: Channels are shaped by frequent moderate floods, not rare catastrophes. Understanding bankfull discharge is essential for river management, restoration and floodplain mapping.
